content: Pneumococcal Disease Surveillance and Trends Feb. 25, 2026 Key points CDC tracks invasive pneumococcal disease (IPD) using 2 surveillance systems. Invasive bacterial disease refers to when bacteria invade parts of the body, like blood, that are normally free from germs. CDC doesn't track non-invasive pneumococcal disease, such as pneumococcal ear infections. Learn about the latest trends in IPD. Data systems National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System Invasive diseases, such as meningitis and bacteremia (bloodstream infections), are the only nationally notifiable diseases caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae bacteria. CDC collects national information about IPD through the National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS). CDC receives NNDSS data each week from state and public health partners. For Everyone National Notifiable Diseases Surveillance System (NNDSS) Active Bacterial Core surveillance CDC collaborates with some state health departments to conduct IPD surveillance. Examples of IPD include: Meningitis Bacteremia Osteomyelitis Septic arthritis Information is collected through Active Bacterial Core surveillance (ABCs) , which is part of CDC's Emerging Infections Program . For Everyone Active Bacterial Core surveillance (ABCs) Bact Facts Interactive You can analyze and visualize ABCs IPD data. Use Bact Facts Interactive How the data are interpreted Disease trends IPD surveillance in the United States began in 1998. IPD rates dramatically declined in children and adults after the United States began using pneumococcal conjugate vaccines (PCVs) in 2000. Temporal pattern Pneumococcal infections are more common during the winter and in early spring when respiratory diseases are more prevalent. Antibiotic resistance Pneumococcal bacteria that cause IPD are not susceptible to one or more classes of antibiotics in more than 40% of cases. Keep Reading Antibiotic-resistant S. pneumoniae Vaccination impact CDC data show that IPD rates in the United States decreased dramatically after introduction of PCVs. Timeline of CDC's PCV Recommendations PCV7: 2000 in children PCV13: 2010 in children; 2012 in adults with risk conditions; 2014-2019 in adults 65 years or older PCV15: 2021 in adults; 2022 in children PCV20: 2021 in adults; 2023 in children Childhood vaccination and disease trends From 1998 through 2021, IPD rates among children less than 5 years old decreased by 95% overall 99% for disease caused by serotypes covered by PCV13 Adult vaccination and disease trends IPD rates in adults decreased after PCVs were used in children. PCV use in children can provide herd immunity and decrease IPD rates in adults. IPD caused by the serotypes covered by 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine (PPSV23) also declined during this time. However, these reductions were due to declines in IPD caused by serotypes in common with PCV13. PPSV23 has been available since 1984. Data reporting View NNDSS infectious disease data tables . View ABCs annual reports for IPD . Data definitions The Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists (CSTE) released the most recent case definition for IPD in 2017. Global trends S. pneumoniae remains a leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children under 5 years old worldwide. The majority of cases and deaths occur in developing countries. Leading cause S. pneumoniae is the leading cause of bacterial pneumonia globally. It accounted for more deaths than all other causes combined in 2016 . Most of these deaths occur in countries in Africa and Asia. Declining rates Gavi, The Vaccine Alliance, has helped many low-income countries introduce a PCV into their national immunization programs. Countries that introduced a PCV have seen large reductions in IPD and pneumonia.
